newsitem.title: Austria: Bombers target Austria minister's step-mother.
newsitem.headline: Bombers target Austria minister's step-mother.

text.p: A letter bomb exploded in Vienna on Monday but the device failed to reach its target, the step-mother of Interior Minister Caspar Einem, the interior ministry said.

A woman -- not Einem's step-mother -- called police after she received the suspicious package. The device exploded after bomb disposal experts took the package away at around 6 p.m. (1700 GMT). No-one was injured in the blast.
"It was addressed to the minister's step-mother Lotte Ingrisch," an interior ministry spokeswoman said.
But the package was incorrectly addressed to Ingrisch's former home which she left a year ago and it did not reach her.
Ingrisch used to write librettos for Einem's father, composer Gottfried von Einem, who died in July, aged 78.
In a first reaction, Caspar Einem, a member of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democratic Party, said his family had been aware it could be a potential letter bomb target.
"They obviously did their homework badly," he told Austrian news agency APA.

No group has yet claimed responsibility for sending the device, but the self-styled Bajuwarian Liberation Army (BLA) has admitted sending more than a score of racially-motivated letter bombs since December 1993, which have injured 12 people.
The bombs have all been aimed at foreigners or figures linked to immigration or refugee issues in Austria and Germany.

"This is the beginning of the sixth series of letter bombs," said Robert Sturm, the chief of the Interior Ministry bomb investigation unit, warning the public to be on their guard for further letter bomb attacks.
Police have also linked the group to the murder of four gypsy men in Oberwart, southeast Austria, in February 1995.
They died instantly when they tried to remove a racist sign reading "Roma (gypsies) back to India" outside their village, setting off a booby-trapped bomb.
Police officials suspect neo-Nazis to be behind the shadowy organisation, and have acknowledged that the devices have been put together by someone with expert knowledge of bombs.

Police chiefs have come under fire for failing to make any arrests connected to the letter bomb campaign or for the gypsy murders. Two neo-Nazis arrested in December 1993 on suspicion of involvement in the attacks were acquitted last December.

Einem said had his step-mother still lived at her former address, the device would have arrived on December 3, the third anniversary of the first letter bomb sent to a priest who worked with refugees.

The post office returned the letter to the sender's address on the package. The perpetrators used an address of an astrological society in Vienna's Favoriten district, Einem said. A member of the society was believed to have discovered the device. Ingrisch is known to have an interest in astrology.
One of the letter bomb blasts ripped off three fingers of former Vienna mayor Helmut Zilk when he opened a letter in his home in December 1993.

Government sources have indicated the BLA may consist of a handful of middle-aged fanatics, believed to be obsessed with reuniting German-speaking peoples in Bavaria, the Alps and along the Danube River -- a distinct region which existed between the sixth and 12th centuries.
